articles.title: Why is Microsoft's outage lasting so long and will emails be lost?
articles.snippet: Microsoft says it is continuing to restore services including Outlook and Teams following a global outage.
articles.full_text:
Why is Microsoft's outage lasting so long and will emails be lost?
- Published
A major Microsoft outage has impacted schools, healthcare systems, businesses, courts and governments around the world.
Services including Teams, Outlook and AI software Copilot, are being restored almost 24 hours since issues first surfaced.
Microsoft said the outage was not a cyber-security incident and was caused by a technical issue. It has apologised for the disruption.
Here's what we know about the services affected and what went wrong.
What happened?
Some Microsoft 365 services have been affected by "connectivity problems" with problems reported in at least 74 countries.
From late on Thursday, customers reported varying levels of access - many were unable to send or receive emails, view certain files or details on their calendar apps.
But some users were able to use Teams, messaging and online meeting functions without issues.
As of Friday afternoon, Microsoft said it had seen "encouraging recovery progress" in Europe and improvement in North America.
The company added that it was focused on "addressing the remaining areas of disruption" but warned "some users may still experience intermittent issues".
In a later statement, the company said it was continuing to see improvements "with email queues significantly reduced and approaching normal levels".
The company attributed the ongoing outage to "elevated load" on its infrastructure, saying it stemmed from an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade.
Will emails affected by the outage ever arrive?
Although services are beginning to resume, Microsoft has warned of continued "intermittent access issues", meaning some users will still struggle to load their inboxes and could experience "delayed email delivery".
In other words, it is not quite safe to assume every email you send is going to arrive in its intended recipient's inbox right away.
Earlier, Microsoft said it would be extending the "timeout window" to 48 hours "to help protect delayed messages as delivery catches up".
The email timeout window refers to the amount of time Outlook will wait to receive an email.
When they do show up, the timestamp will be when they were delivered rather than when they were sent.
Why has it taken so long to fix?
Although email service Outlook appears to be resuming, the outage has so far lasted for more than 20 hours - in outage terms that is considered a long time.
Prof James Ferryman from the University of Reading's department of computer science said the details the company has disclosed provide some clues.
"What Microsoft has told us is that the part of its servers that sets up secure connections is getting swamped, and once that happens the server just stops answering," he said.
"The trouble is that this kind of failure snowballs.
"One server falls over, its work gets passed to the next one, and meanwhile huge numbers of phones and laptops keep trying to get back in.
"You can't just turn it all back on at once. You have to bring it back bit by bit."
The challenge is therefore not just fixing the fault, but managing the huge surge of devices trying to reconnect once services start coming back online.
Gergely Orosz, a former leading software engineer at several major tech companies including Skype and Uber, said this could be the "most disruptive" business email outage "of all time".
He said it was still difficult to know just how many people have been affected by the disruption, but added he "cannot recall" an outage over business email ever taking this long to return to normal.
Australian cyber-security expert Troy Hunt told the BBC the outage could have far-reaching consequences.
"Microsoft is a massive part of the internet backbone and reminds us how critical email still is.
"Not only does this outage affect many people's ability to work but also things like the ability to communicate about appointments, purchase things that need verification, create or access accounts and services," he said.
In a statement, Microsoft said it was "deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners.
"We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously. We are seeing broad recovery and stability across our services."
How many people have been affected?
More than 430 million people use Microsoft 365 apps according to Microsoft's website. The full scale of the outage has not been confirmed.
Microsoft 365 is used by companies worldwide and is expected to have a knock-on effect to other services.
Tech giants OpenAI and Anthropic both earlier reported problems as a result of the outage.
ChatGPT-maker OpenAI said it was investigating an issue affecting its connections to Microsoft's services, which had caused some tools to not work as expected.
From city governments in the US to Australian spy agencies, disruption across the globe has been widespread.
Courts from Los Angeles to Texas earlier warned that communications might be delayed.
In Canada, the public broadcaster CBC reported that a healthcare network running several hospitals in Toronto was experiencing email issues, but that patient care was not affected.
The government of Japan also said its shared IT platform had been disrupted.
Across the UK, GP surgeries, pharmacies, police and schools have been affected by the outage.
Some GP surgeries had urged patients not to submit messages via their website while police forces were also earlier asking the public to call if they want to make a report.

articles.title: Rosenberg: Uncompromising Putin ups demands for peace with Ukraine
articles.snippet: The fact the question of European security now features in discussions is viewed in Moscow as a victory, BBC Russia Editor Steve Rosenberg says.
articles.full_text:
Rosenberg: Uncompromising Putin ups demands for peace with Ukraine
- Published
Russia's President Vladimir Putin says he wishes "eternal peace" for Ukraine.
That is the same Russian president who ordered the full-scale invasion of Russia's neighbour nearly five years ago and who continues to reject the idea of a comprehensive ceasefire.
And what, in Moscow's view, is a prerequisite for peace?
The Kremlin spelt it out after talks with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner: "A new, long-term architecture of indivisible security and peace."
Translated from Kremlin-speak, it means Moscow wants to change the security set-up of Europe in a way that benefits Russia.
What Russia is pushing for is, potentially, the biggest change to European security arrangements since the end of the Cold War.
The Kremlin has put back on the table its controversial proposal from December 2021 â the "draft treaties" with the US and Nato which would not only have put the brakes on the alliance's eastward enlargement by giving Moscow cast-iron guarantees that, for instance, Ukraine and Georgia would never be allowed to join, but also rolled back Nato military infrastructure from countries of central and eastern Europe which became Nato members following the dissolution of the Soviet Union.
Western leaders dismissed such demands as an unacceptable Russian ultimatum. Two months later Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
The "draft treaties" were put away. Now they are out of the geopolitical filing cabinet, and being quoted again by the Kremlin.
What is more, Yuri Ushakov, Putin's foreign policy aide, has suggested that Moscow is about to "add certain new considerations" to its list of demands in light of Western efforts "to inflict a strategic defeat on Russia".
That does not mean, of course, that Western governments will accept them.
But the fact that the question of European security is featuring now in discussions on Ukraine is viewed here as a victory for Moscow.
"In December 2021 Russia actively proposed that Nato rethink the security system in Europe," wrote newspaper Komsomolskaya Pravda earlier this week.
"Our proposals were almost laughed at.
"Having secured one victory by forcing the West to think about security, our diplomats need a second by making the West heed Russia's concerns about Nato enlargement."
The EU's top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, has called Russia's demands for a new European security architecture a "trap" designed to "shift attention away from a ceasefire".
"The sequencing of Ukraine-Russia talks is important," Kallas wrote on social media. "The priority should be securing a ceasefire, followed by a peace agreement. Only then can there be discussions on Europe's wider security architecture."
Europe's problem is that, right now, it is not at the table.
Moscow has had no desire to give it a chair. It has slammed European leaders for their military support for Kyiv and tough stance on Russia.
This week's peace talks in Abu Dhabi involved Ukraine, Russia and the US.
After his discussions in Moscow, Witkoff indicated that Putin had agreed to the idea of European representatives joining the next round of Ukraine peace talks.
But on Friday the Kremlin indicated a final decision on European participation had not been taken.
"Once we understand their true intentions and their readiness to facilitate the peace process, then it will be possible to take a decision about dialogue on Ukraine in a wider format," said Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov.

Europe's security 'fundamentally reshaped' by war in Ukraine
- Published1 day ago
Inside devastated front-line city that Russia wants Ukraine to give up
- Published3 days ago
And what of Putin?
At the talks with Witkoff and Kushner he was sounding uncompromising and confident.
You can see why.
The Americans are knocking at his door and seeking a deal and the Europeans are contemplating contacts with him. Last month the leaders of Norway and Finland reached out and called him.
And next week in Shenzhen, China, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation summit, Putin may have a separate meeting with Donald Trump and Xi Jinping. Russian media are already comparing them to the "Big Three" - Stalin, Roosevelt and Churchill - who met in 1945 to reorganise post-World War Two Europe.
And yet, after nearly five years of war, Russia has suffered huge losses on the battlefield.
The Russian economy is under increasing pressure.
Ukrainian drone strikes continue to target Russian oil refineries, sparking fears of new fuel shortages.
But, so far, none of this has convinced the Kremlin leader to end the fighting.

articles.title: Nvidia scandal fallout widens as Trump's treasury secretary blames cabinet colleague
articles.snippet: Scott Bessent suggests Howard Lutnick’s commerce department failed to ban exports of Nvidia's chips to a firm thought to have links with China.
articles.full_text:
Pressure grows on Trump's Commerce Secretary Lutnick in fallout from Nvidia scandal
- Published
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has blamed the Commerce Department, run by Howard Lutnick, for failing to properly oversee the export of high-spec Nvidia chips, as the fallout from the scandal widens.
There is growing pressure on Lutnick across the political spectrum to explain his department's actions.
Jensen Huang was ousted as Nvidia CEO after revelations he had an affair with a businesswoman who was also allegedly a Chinese spy.
Megaspeed, the firm she worked for, had been probed by US government agencies over suspicions it had been smuggling Nvidia chips into China, reports said, but is not on a list of firms that US companies are prevented from working with.
Bessent told CNBC several agencies "were in favour of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months".
"But Commerce has the pen... and you will have to ask them about their internal process," he added.
Bessent's comments come after Lutnick was called to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month over the Commerce Department's role in allowing Nvidia to export its advanced chips.
Other congressional committees have asked both Lutnick and his department to retain all records relating to Nvidia and Huang.
Bessent said he was "frustrated" by delays in putting the company on the export control list and reports of leakage of AI chips into China.
"President Trump made it very clear that China should not receive any Nvidia chips above H100s, so any leakage is very frustrating because it hurts our great companies in the AI race, because it gives the Chinese an advantage," he said.
Last year, the Commerce Department had been investigating Megaspeed over suspicions it had been smuggling some of Nvidia's advanced AI chips into China, according to the New York Times. Megaspeed has been contacted for comment.
There was also pressure on the Commerce Department to add it to the list, but separate reporting in the Financial Times said the department was delaying efforts to have the cloud computing firm included.
However, Bessent also pointed the finger at Nvidia.
"The story has been thus far of Jensen Huang's personal foibles," he told CNBC's Squawk Box programme, external.
"The real story here should be: Did Nvidia know their client, and was there a robust effort at Nvidia to make sure that there was no leakage and that they were selling to what were obviously pass-through shell companies?
"It's important that anyone at the company there be held accountable for that."
How a sex scandal at Nvidia is putting pressure on the White House
- Published6 hours ago
How AI visionary Jensen Huang was undone by his own bad decisions
- Published1 day ago
Huang has been summoned to testify before the Senate Banking Committee about his affair with the former Megaspeed executive, who is suspected of being a Chinese spy.
The Commerce Secretary has also been summoned to appear before the committee in December.
"Recent reports raise serious concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive US technology," committee chairman, Republican Senator Tim Scott posted on X.
Democrats on key congressional committees have asked the Commerce Department and Lutnick to keep all records relating to decisions to allow Nvidia to sell its advanced AI chips to Chinese companies, including all their communications with or about Nvidia and Jensen Huang.
Ways and Means Committee Ranking Member Richard E. Neal and Senate Finance Committee Ranking Member Ron Wyden are starting investigations into the way Nvidia was allowed to sell these chips.
According to Neal and Wyden, Nvidia's advanced H200 chips could be sold to Chinese firms if they were first imported from their manufacturing facility in Taiwan into America for inspection.
A 25% tariff - a levy that is paid to the federal government - was imposed on those chips, under a section of the Trade Act that Neal and Wyden say is meant to allow the US president to take action against imports that risk national security.
"Trump's use of the statute appears to have done the opposite, undermining US national security and putting Americans at risk," they said.

articles.title: German spies handed new powers to tackle 'hybrid threats' from abroad
articles.snippet: German reforms mean foreign and domestic intelligence services will have greater powers to combat espionage, terrorism and sabotage.
articles.full_text:
German spies handed new powers to tackle 'hybrid threats' from abroad
- Published
Germany's foreign and domestic intelligence services are to be given greater powers to combat espionage, terrorism and sabotage after the country's parliament, the Bundestag, approved a major overhaul of its legislation.
Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt, who championed the bill, has called it a "reform of the century", necessary because of the increasing threats from foreign powers.
But the Left Party's security spokeswoman, Clara BÃ¼nger, said Dobrindt was creating a new German secret police.
The legislation gives numerous new powers to Germany's BND federal intelligence service, and its BfV domestic service, the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution.
In the Bundestag, 309 MPs voted in favour of the new law on intelligence services, while 190 voted against and 71 abstained.
For historical reasons, German intelligence has mainly focused on gathering information rather than acting on it.
In future, German spies working for the BND, which is responsible for foreign intelligence, will be able to conduct covert operations abroad, including sabotage.
This could include paralysing the servers of state-sponsored hacker groups, disrupting disinformation networks, or even disrupting supply chains for weapons.
Agents for the domestic intelligence service, the BfV, will no longer to be limited to gathering information. For the first time they will be able to take protective action against property and IT systems, if specific threats are identified.
That means they will be allowed to dismantle or break explosives or weapons, divert or block data flows during cyber-attacks, delete or falsify data stored for malicious purposes, and plant false information on those involved.
Sabotage suspect held in Germany after spate of attacks on power grid
- Published8 September
Germany says Russia behind Leipzig airport drone attack
- Published2 September
Under certain conditions, BfV agents will also be permitted to enter homes covertly. However, the measure must always be authorised in advance.
They will also be given wider powers of digital surveillance, including monitoring encrypted telecommunications and carrying out online searches. They will also be allowed to use AI-supported data analysis and biometric image matching on the internet.
The government says the reform is needed because of an increase in foreign espionage, particularly from Russia, China and Iran.
"We are the target of hybrid threats," said Dobrindt. "Germany is a theatre of operations for terrorism, extremism and foreign powers."
In August, a drone carrying an explosive device was discovered at Leipzig Airport, close to Ukrainian cargo planes. However, it failed to explode as the bomb's detonator was apparently faulty.
German authorities say Russia was behind the attack.
The new law has been bitterly criticised by some opposition politicians, even though Dobrindt has said it is "madness" to think it means that Germany is creating a new secret police.
And Clara BÃ¼nger from the Left Party told public broadcaster ARD that the new law was "a monsterâ¦ summoning ghosts that we will probably never be able to get rid of".
The separation between the police and the secret service, she warned, was "being eroded" - and BÃ¼nger said that had been a lesson learned from the Nazi era.
"This means the secret service is being granted executive powers and will not only be allowed to act pre-emptively, but will also be granted police powers."
However, Sonja Eichwede of the centre-left SPD, which is part of Germany's governing coalition, said the reforms would make a significant contribution to ensuring the country's democracy was "robust and resilient".

articles.title: African Miss Universe beauty queens in limbo as US visa restrictions bite
articles.snippet: Hall has been seeking a US visa in South Africa as other African beauty queens face similar hurdles.
articles.full_text:
African Miss Universe beauty queens in limbo as US visa restrictions bite
- Published
Miss Universe Zimbabwe Roseanna Hall and several other contestants from Africa could miss this year's competition in Puerto Rico as they race to secure a US visa.
Hall is due to represent Zimbabwe at the 75th edition of the Miss Universe pageant, with the winner set to be crowned on 24 November. But she has yet to obtain a visa to travel to the US territory.
"We have been back and forth, trying to get my visa approved," Hall said in a video posted on her Instagram page.
Hall is not the only African contestant to be affected by the restrictions. Zambia has withdrawn its representative, Pamela Mubanga, from the competition because of US travel restrictions.
Contestants began arriving in Puerto Rico on 8 November for registration, fittings and other pre-pageant activities, putting pressure on Hall, and others including the representative from South Sudan, to secure their visas.
"Officially, today is the day I was supposed to be leaving for Puerto Rico for the 75th edition of Miss Universe," Hall said.
Zimbabwe is among 19 countries subject to partial US travel restrictions introduced under the Presidential Proclamation 10998, which took effect on 1 January 2026.
The measures suspend the issuance of visitor, student and exchange visas, as well as immigrant visas, to nationals of the affected countries. They also impose restrictions on other categories of non-immigrant visas.
In a statement, the Miss Universe organization in Zambia said Mubanga's situation was a consequence of the travel restrictions rather than individual circumstances.
"Unlike situations where a contestant's visa is denied due to personal circumstances, documentation or organisational challenges, Mubanga's situation is linked to the United States' presidential travel restriction affecting Zambia and other African countries," the statement read.
Mubanga, 25, a registered nurse, was crowned Miss Universe Zambia on 8 October and was due to represent the country at the international pageant.
The statement said five other African countries faced similar difficulties, although it did not name them.
Hall said she shared their concerns, adding that she had spent the past few weeks in South Africa trying to secure her visa.
"I am not alone in this predicament. Some of my African sisters are facing the same predicament, and I know exactly what they are going through," she said.
Miss Universe South Sudan also expressed uncertainty about her participation, commenting on Hall's video: "It is 50/50 whether we will make it, Miss Universe."
In another video posted three days earlier, Hall said she was still hoping to make it to Puerto Rico.
She captioned the video: "The fight to get Zimbabwe to Puerto Rico continues,"
The pageant's final is scheduled to take place at the JosÃ© Miguel Agrelot Coliseum in San Juan.

articles.title: Democratic Senate leader Schumer set to face leadership challenge
articles.snippet: Maryland Senator Van Hollen says "new leadership" is needed for Democrats following the party's recent midterm successes.
articles.full_text:
Democratic Senate leader Schumer set to face leadership challenge
- Published
US Senator Chuck Schumer is facing a challenge to his position as US Senate majority leader from his fellow Democratic Senator Chris Van Hollen, as the party prepares to take control of Congress after sweeping the midterm elections.
Van Hollen, 67, said in a post on X on Thursday that Americans voted for change earlier this month and "to deliver, we need new leadership".
Schumer, 75, has led Democrats in the chamber since 2017, serving as both majority and minority leader. He was first elected to the Senate in 1999.
Following the midterms earlier this month, his position has come under pressure by some left-wing Democrats who see him as too moderate and part of the party establishment.
Responding to the challenge, Schumer, who represents New York, said he welcomes "any discussion about the future of our caucus and the important work ahead".
He added that he is "proud of what we've accomplished together" in the midterms, and he has "the votes to continue as Democratic leader".
The vote on Senate leader will be held behind closed doors in early December and the winner will assume the role on 4 January, when Democrats take control of both the Senate and the House of Representatives after their midterms successes.
The move by Van Hollen, who represents Maryland, marks the most significant step by a high-profile Democrat to challenge the party's existing leadership following last week's midterms victory.
Announcing his plans to run on X, he wrote that Americans had called on the party to "unrig an economy rigged against working people".
In recent years, Van Hollen has taken positions popular with those on the left of his party.
In 2024, he supported restricting weapons shipments to Israel and criticised the Biden administration over its role in the war in Gaza.
In an interview with MS NOW, Van Hollen - who has served in the Senate for nearly a decade - acknowledged that he is an "underdog" but added that he believes the race is "very much in flux".
Independent Senator Bernie Sanders and Democratic Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed have both publicly come out in support of Van Hollen - while others have also called for new leadership.
In a post on X, Sanders said he believes Van Hollen "will stand up to powerful special interests, take on the billionaire class and fight for working families".
El-Sayed said the challenger would bring "bold leadership" and lead with both "courage and experience".
Others Democrats have publicly backed Schumer.
Senator Jacky Rosen of Nevada said: "He has the experience and the fight to continue leading our diverse caucus at this crucial moment".
Senator Kirsten Gillibrand said: "You will see, despite all the grumblings, enormous gratitude for the hard work he has done to get us to this position."

articles.title: UN watchdog 'increasingly concerned' over uninspected Iran nuclear site
articles.snippet: It says it has never been able to visit a uranium enrichment plant at Isfahan which Iran announced over a year ago.
articles.full_text:
UN watchdog 'increasingly concerned' over uninspected Iran nuclear site
- Published
The UN's nuclear watchdog has said it is "increasingly concerned" about a nuclear facility in Iran which it has not been allowed to inspect.
Iran informed the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) of plans to set up the uranium enrichment plant in the city of Isfahan a day before Israel began attacking its nuclear sites last June. The US joined the strikes later that month.
In a report seen by news agencies, the IAEA said it does not know the exact location or whether it contains nuclear material.
Since the start of the latest war, Iran has restricted IAEA inspectors' access to its nuclear sites, preventing the agency from verifying its enriched uranium stockpile.
Under a 2015 nuclear deal, Iran agreed to limit its enriched uranium stockpile to 300kg and enrichment to 3.67% purity. It subsequently exceeded both.
Before the June 2025 strikes, it had accumulated an estimated 441kg enriched to 60%, close to weapons grade.
The nuclear complex at Isfahan suffered extensive damage in US and Israeli strikes, particularly the parts above the ground. The condition of its underground facilities is not clear.
The IAEA believes much of Iran's highly enriched uranium was stored there.
"The Agency's lack of information about [Iran's] nuclear material and access to facilities to verify it is a matter of serious proliferation concern... and needs to be rectified with the utmost urgency," it said in the latest report.
Iran announced plans for the Isfahan Fuel Enrichment Plant (IFEP) on 12 June 2025, shortly after an IAEA resolution which declared Iran had failed to meet its nuclear safeguards obligations.
Iran initially agreed to allow inspectors to visit the facility, but the inspection was cancelled after Israel launched attacks the following day.
The IAEA's latest calls come almost a year after it made a similar appeal to Iran. At the time it said it had only inspected some of the 13 nuclear facilities that were "unaffected" by the attacks and none of the seven that were.
The US and Israel said they attacked Iran's nuclear sites to prevent it developing nuclear weapons - something Iran has consistently denied seeking. It says its nuclear programme is for peaceful civilian purposes only.

articles.title: The fight over Canadian steelworker jobs
articles.source: Al Jazeera – Breaking News, World News and Video from Al Jazeera
articles.snippet: Stelco's US owner blames Trump's tariffs for layoffs, but its support for those same tariffs has raised questions.
articles.full_text:
The fight over Canadian steelworker jobs
Stelco’s US owner blames Trump’s tariffs for layoffs, but its support for those same tariffs has raised questions.
Hamilton, Ontario, Canada – Chelsey Masteij had heard layoffs might be coming at Stelco, so she decided to use up some of her vacation days. She was making the most of the time off with her new dog when she got a call telling her not to come back to work.
The 34-year-old had spent years trying to break into the male-dominated steel industry before finally landing a job at the company’s Hamilton plant about three years ago.

She started as a general labourer in the cold-rolling department, later training to operate cranes and taking on shifts in the coke ovens.
The work was gruelling and physically demanding, but Masteij grew to love the routine and the close-knit community of coworkers she came to consider family. When she shared photos of herself with Al Jazeera, all in protective gear at the plant, she joked that she hardly had any pictures outside of work.
Masteij thought she might stay at Stelco until retirement. Instead, she was laid off on October 9.
The news hit hard, and she spent much of the next two weeks sleeping.
“I was in a complete mess,” she told Al Jazeera, her voice cracking as she recalled the experience. “I was kind of depressed.”
Now, instead of working 12-hour shifts, Masteij spends much of her time at home, cutting back on expenses while she collects employment insurance.
Masteij is among hundreds of Canadian steelworkers facing layoffs after Stelco’s American owner, Cleveland-Cliffs, announced in late September that it would temporarily shut down parts of its operations in Hamilton and Nanticoke, Ontario.
Stelco blames the move on United States President Donald Trump’s tariffs, which it says have made it harder to sell Canadian steel to US customers, and on competition from cheaper foreign steel entering Canada.
But government officials and plant workers, including Masteij, are not convinced that is the whole story.
“Right now, there are a lot of lies going on with what’s happened,” Masteij said.
While US tariffs have hurt the Canadian steel industry, the union representing Stelco workers questions whether Cleveland-Cliffs is using difficult market conditions to serve its own business interests, with Canadian workers paying the price.
“Everyone knows we’re being used as pawns, that these layoffs weren’t necessary,” said Ron Wells, president of United Steelworkers Local 1005, speaking to Al Jazeera at his Hamilton office.
The pressures facing Stelco
In June 2025, Trump doubled tariffs on steel and aluminium imports, including from Canada, to 50 percent, making them more expensive for US buyers.
According to Stelco, Canada’s exports of cold-rolled and coated steel to the US – used to make everything from cars to building materials – fell by 58 percent in the second quarter of 2026 compared with the quarterly average before the trade war.
But demand has also fallen in Canada, where the auto industry, a major buyer of the cold-rolled steel produced at the Hamilton plant, has also been hit hard by Trump’s tariffs, said Colin Mang, an assistant professor of economics at McMaster University in Hamilton.
“When they say that there is less demand for the product coming out of the Hamilton mill, that is correct,” Mang told Al Jazeera.
But it is not just Trump’s tariffs that Cleveland-Cliffs blames for Stelco’s problems.
During a July earnings call, CEO Lourenco Goncalves warned that the company might scale back production in Canada unless Ottawa did more to protect its steel industry from imports.
“And that will have consequences for employment in Canada, but will have a positive financial impact on Stelco and on Cleveland-Cliffs,” he said.
That was the first time Wells had heard jobs might be at risk. The union later offered to help Cleveland-Cliffs lobby Ottawa for stronger protections against foreign steel imports, believing Canadian workers might have more sway with the government.
“They never took us up on our offer,” Wells said.
Instead, the next call brought news of the layoffs.
As of Saturday, 175 workers at Stelco’s Hamilton plant had received layoff notices, with the announced cuts expected to affect up to 500 workers there and in Nanticoke.
Late last month, about 30 attended an information session the union organised in Hamilton, where they could learn about employment insurance and retraining opportunities.
Many were frustrated by the lack of clarity about how long the shutdown would last.
Some asked how their benefits would compare to their wages, while others wondered whether they would qualify for the full amount.
For workers who had spent decades at Stelco, another daunting prospect loomed: having to look for work for the first time in the digital era, competing for jobs with younger applicants as they neared retirement.
Some are already considering heading out west to find work.
“It’s hard for them to make those decisions,” Wells said, describing what he had been hearing from members. “Do I leave my family, go out west, make some money? Because they don’t know how long this is going to be.”
Masteij worries about what that could mean for Hamilton, a city where generations of families have worked in steelmaking, an industry that has shaped its identity for more than a century.
“I’m a steel city girl, and I can’t imagine the city without steel manufacturing,” she said. “We are losing tradesmen.”
Were the layoffs necessary?
But as workers grapple with what the layoffs mean for their families and their city, the union has been asking another question: whether these layoffs needed to happen at all – and it is not alone.
The US company has come under fire from the Canadian government, which is threatening legal action, accusing it of breaking promises it made when it bought Stelco in 2024.
Those included keeping at least the same number of unionised jobs and most non-unionised jobs in Canada, and pushing for trade policies that would benefit the steel industries in both Canada and the US.
Cleveland-Cliffs denies violating the agreement, saying it expects to meet its employment commitments for the year. It also maintains the layoffs are needed to “ensure the survival of Stelco” amid US tariffs, weaker demand and competition from cheaper foreign steel.
But the union and the government point to Stelco’s recent financial performance. Earlier this month, Goncalves reported the company’s strongest quarter since the acquisition.
“Mr Goncalves is not a victim,” Canadian Industry Minister Melanie Joly told Canada’s public broadcaster CBC, pointing to the company’s earnings. “He’s never made so much money.”
Experts have also challenged Goncalves’s claim that Canadian steelmakers are struggling because of “an avalanche of imports”.
Mang points out that nearly 80 percent of Canada’s cold-rolled steel imports come from the US, as does about half of the galvanised and painted steel coming into the country.
“What he’s trying to sell people on is the idea that there’s all this European or Asian steel coming into Canada,” he said. “This stuff is coming from his own country.”
The union and the government have also asked why, as Goncalves pushes for stronger protections in Canada against foreign steel, he has also been a vocal supporter of Trump’s tariffs on Canadian steel.
In testimony to US lawmakers in January, Goncalves argued that no country, including Canada, should be exempted from the steel tariffs. In an interview with Politico last year, he said he was “very happy” with the 50 percent tariffs on steel imports, adding, “I have my fingerprints on that 50 percent.”
Two countries, one company
For Wells, the irony is that Goncalves helped create the same conditions Cleveland-Cliffs now blames for the layoffs. He believes the company is using Canadian workers to pressure Ottawa to impose more restrictions on foreign steel, while also helping Trump argue that his tariffs are working.
Mang explained why Goncalves’ seemingly contradictory position might make sense for Cleveland-Cliffs.
“He wants trade barriers in both countries to seal off their domestic markets from each other and also from the rest of the world,” Mang said, “so that his companies in each country can benefit in their own domestic markets.”
Cleveland-Cliffs has been under growing pressure from Ottawa, which gave the company 15 days from October 22 to honour its commitments to Canadian workers or face legal action.
Amid that pressure, comments Goncalves made to CBC late last month appeared to support the union’s suspicions that the layoffs have less to do with tough market conditions and more to do with Cleveland-Cliffs’ broader business interests.
Asked why he supported tariffs on Canadian steel despite promises to protect workers and advocate for the Canadian steel industry when Cleveland-Cliffs bought Stelco, he said: “I bought Stelco because I could not afford anymore having Stelco flooding the market here in the United States to the detriment of my own company.”
The admission caught the attention of Joly, who said the comments could strengthen the government’s case against Cleveland-Cliffs if Goncalves meant that he had bought Stelco to keep its Canadian operations idle. She added that Ottawa could force the company to sell its Canadian assets.
On November 6, as Ottawa’s 15-day deadline expired, Joly asked Canada’s Competition Bureau to investigate the 2024 acquisition and whether the company’s conduct violated Canadian competition law.
“If negotiations and acquisition were conducted in bad faith, Canadians deserve to know. The company needs to face the consequences,” she said in a statement.
Cleveland-Cliffs maintains that it has complied with its obligations under the Investment Canada Act.
Goncalves has rejected the prospect of a forced sale but suggested he might sell Stelco himself in a year.
“I will sell the company after we operate the company for a while, and now that I know that I’m persona non grata in Canada, I will do that,” he told CBC.
In a statement to The Canadian Press news agency late last month, he said he hoped to bring laid-off workers back before Christmas.
“It will depend on Canadian customers buying Canadian steel, made by Stelco,” he said.
Al Jazeera contacted Cleveland-Cliffs for comment on the union’s allegations and Goncalves’s remarks.
What comes next for workers?
For Masteij, even as she waits to hear whether she will be recalled, she is preparing for the possibility that her time at Stelco is done. Her low seniority means she would be one of the last to be called back.
Masteij plans to use the time she is eligible for employment insurance to take a heavy equipment training programme, hoping it will open the door to other opportunities and give her something to focus on. The training could also help her if she returns to Stelco, which is still what she is hoping for.
For Wells, what is especially frustrating is how the company is treating workers, given the years of hard work and sacrifices many have made in their jobs.
“It’s not glamorous. You work shifts, nights, days, in the hot and the cold,” he said. “Our members miss Christmas meals with their families or their kids’ hockey games because they’re expected to work.”
“And that’s why this is particularly tough because that loyalty isn’t being repaid,” Wells added. “It’s actually being exploited, if anything.”
He worries about what a drawn-out legal battle could mean for those workers.
“Our members don’t have a lot of time,” he said. “We’re hoping things get settled as soon as possible.”

Car bombings in Russia kill military officer, injure ex-Ukraine PM adviser
Moscow blames Kyiv for a series of car bombings that have targeted people linked to the war with Ukraine.
A car bombing in Moscow has critically injured an adviser to Ukraine’s former prime minister a day after a similar attack killed a military officer in St Petersburg.
The explosion on Friday was the latest in a series of bombings and shootings that have targeted people involved in the fighting in Ukraine. Moscow has blamed Kyiv for the attacks.

The Moscow explosion struck a car driven by Sergei Zavorotnyi, who previously worked as an adviser to former Ukrainian Prime Minister Mykola Azarov, according to Russia’s Investigative Committee.
Zavorotnyi was hospitalised with injuries, the committee added. It did not identify possible suspects pending a criminal inquiry.
Azarov served as prime minister under Ukraine’s Moscow-friendly President Viktor Yanukovych, who was forced from office by protesters and fled to Russia in February 2014.
Azarov, who also lives in Russia, told state-run TV that he was “shocked” by the attack that left his former adviser critically injured. He said he believes Zavorotnyi was targeted because of his criticism of the Ukrainian government.
Zavorotnyi. 72, had worked as a journalist for Russia’s daily Komsomolskaya Pravda before becoming Azarov’s adviser. He wrote a book about Yanukovych’s ouster and ran an online outlet critical of Ukrainian authorities.
Russia’s REN TV channel said he lost his left arm, suffered multiple other injuries and was in a coma after the explosion.
Explosive devices triggered remotely
Al Jazeera’s Yulia Shapovalova, reporting from Moscow, said an explosive device was reportedly planted under the man’s car and detonated remotely as he was driving on Friday.
“The investigative committee has already launched a criminal case into this explosion,” she said.
A day earlier, in St Petersburg, a military serviceman was killed by a bomb in his vehicle, according to Russia’s Investigative Committee. It did not identify the victim or say who could be behind the bombing.
The Fontanka news outlet said Thursday’s victim was a colonel, while other Russian online media said the victim was a senior air force officer.
Shapovalova said preliminary reports indicated that the victim was a military serviceman, rather than a colonel of the Russian Air Force.
Like the attack on Friday, he was also driving the car when the bomb went off, she added.
“In both cases an explosive device was triggered remotely, and it was planted under their car,” Shapovalova said. “Here in Russia, all the attacks are considered to be orchestrated by the Ukrainian side.”
Ukrainian authorities have not commented on either bombing.

Sixth victim confirmed in DC condo-related shooting in US, police say
Police confirm sixth victim in DC condo shooting; suspect dead after barricading himself and starting a fire.
Police have said a sixth person was shot on Thursday morning in Washington, DC, bringing the toll to one person killed and five wounded in an attack they believe was linked to a dispute over maintenance issues in a condo building.
In an updated statement, the Metropolitan Police Department said investigators had found a sixth victim, a woman, after officers initially located five other victims.

She was conscious and breathing with a “non-life-threatening gunshot graze wound”.
“The victim self-treated the wound,” police said.
Two women and two men were taken to hospital, all conscious and breathing.
James Stuart, the 46-year-old manager of the building in which the suspect lived, died at the scene.
Police believe the suspect, a 55-year-old doctor named Matt Wade Lambert, targeted Stuart while Stuart was doing his morning workout at the gym.
The shooting started just before 8am local time (13:00 GMT) at a VIDA Fitness gym in the city’s Logan Circle neighbourhood, about a mile north of the White House.
Police said Lambert shot Stuart inside the gym on the ground floor of the building before going back to his apartment on the seventh floor and firing on people below from his patio.
Five others, some of whom had been working at a construction site across the street. Police have not detailed the circumstances in which the sixth victim was shot.
The shootings unfolded in less than five minutes, according to interim police chief Jeffery Carroll.
Lambert then barricaded himself inside his apartment, where he talked to police negotiators over the phone. Police say he fired at least twice through the door while officers were outside, but no officers were injured.
He also broke the gas line connected to his fireplace and started a fire, which the building’s sprinkler system contained.
Police said Lambert spent most of the conversation with negotiators talking about the dispute with building management.
“Most of the conversation was about the homeowners associations and challenges with that,” said Carroll.
“While our negotiators were communicating with the suspect, they did hear a single gunshot,” he said, adding that Lambert then stopped talking.
When tactical officers forced their way into the apartment, they found him dead from an apparent self-inflicted gunshot wound.
Police said inside the apartment, they found a shotgun, a rifle, and a handgun, all of which had been used in the shooting.
According to court records cited by The Associated Press, Lambert had filed a lawsuit alleging that he had not been able to enjoy his penthouse since 2024 because of mould, moisture and water problems that began after work had been done on the building’s exterior.
The lawsuit was ongoing, and Lambert appeared to have shared details of the dispute, including photos and an engineering report on an X account called ofMiceandMold.
His lawyer, Joel Braithwaite, told reporters on Thursday that the condo where Lambert had lived since 2017 looked like “a warzone” and that Lambert had spent more than $300,000 on the lawsuit.

US Treasury warns against rate hikes during US-Iran war energy ‘shock’
Despite Treasury’s Scott Bessent’s remarks, financial tracker CME Fed Watch forecasts rate hike in December likely.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has called on the Federal Reserve not to hike interest rates because of an “energy supply shock” tied to the US-led conflict with Iran.
“I think the Fed should understand that this is an energy supply shock,” while the underlying US economy is very strong, Bessent said in an interview on CNBC on Friday.
Recommended Stories

- list 2 of 4US Treasury sanctions eight Canadian money exchange firms over Iran ties
- list 3 of 4US Treasury chief Bessent moved to military base after ‘Iranian threats’
- list 4 of 4Bessent’s relocation: From US to EU, is Iran bringing war to Western soil?
“So I think that to hike too much into an energy supply shock when it’s coming down, these are very noisy numbers,” he said. “The Fed’s supposed to look into the future, not look in the rearview mirror.”
The central bank opted to maintain interest rates during its last policy meeting, leaving them at 3.75 to 4 percent. CME FedWatch, which tracks the likelihood of monetary policy decisions, forecasts an 89.4 percent chance that rates will be raised to 4.00–4.25 percent at the next meeting, scheduled for December 9.
Despite pressure from the White House to cut interest rates, the Federal Reserve has held them steady amid inflationary pressures stemming from the US-Israeli war on Iran. Since the conflict began, the Fed has maintained rates five times and raised them once.
Much of that pressure has come from rising energy prices. By September, energy prices had climbed 20.4 percent year over year. Although October’s energy price data has since been released, the Labour Department was unable to collect data in October 2025 because of last year’s government shutdown. As a result, it cannot provide a year-over-year comparison for October 2026.
Bessent’s remarks come amid a stronger-than-expected US jobs report, which bolsters the case for rate hikes. The US economy added 165,000 jobs in October, according to the Labour Department’s release last Friday.
“I’m not going to tell the Fed what to do. I am going to say they should have an open mind,” Bessent said.
The Fed made three rate cuts over the same period last year, he noted.
“And now to reverse just based on an energy supply shock, a reversal in a dramatic way isn’t something that I would do if I were on the Fed. But I’m not on the Fed.”
Feeling the cost
Bessent’s remarks come as some top Fed officials are pushing for the opposite. On Tuesday, Fed Governor Christopher Waller said he planned to support a quarter-point increase at the Fed’s December 8-9 meeting unless the core consumer price index — one of the central bank’s key measures for assessing the rate of inflation — came in at 0.3 percent or more.
“In that case, I believe a 50-basis-point hike in the policy rate should be considered at the December meeting,” he said at a conference in London hosted by King’s Business School and the Money Macro and Finance Society.
The CPI report subsequently came out, showing a 0.4 percent monthly increase.
Consumers are feeling the rising costs at the petrol pump, as prices are declining but remain high. The average price for a gallon of petrol is $3.87 ($1.02 per litre), down from $4.34 ($1.14 per litre)this time a month ago, but still well above the $2.98 ($0.79 per litre) price recorded on February 28, when the US and Israel first struck Iran.

articles.title: Judges close part of ICC Afghanistan investigations that could look at US troops
articles.snippet: The International Criminal Court will close investigations into Afghanistan that previously looked at alleged crimes by U.S. troops and focus only on actions of the Taliban.
articles.full_text:
Judges at the International Criminal Court have issued a decision to formally close part of the prosecutor’s investigations into Afghanistan that previously looked at alleged crimes by U.S. troops and to focus only on actions of the Taliban since 2021, court documents show.
The decision by the chamber formally closes not only the line of inquiry into alleged crimes by U.S. troops, which had already lain dormant since 2021, but also a probe into the Islamic State Khorasan (ISIS-K) militia. The office of the prosecutor told Reuters on Friday it had appealed the decision but could not give further details.
It is the latest step in a legal tussle between prosecutors and judges about the Afghanistan case, and comes after the United States issued institutional sanctions against the court, citing U.S. opposition to arrest warrants issued for Israeli officials and the investigation into actions of U.S. soldiers in Afghanistan.
This year, judges ordered prosecutors to split their Afghanistan inquiries into two separate probes — one focusing on the alleged crimes committed by the Taliban since 2021, and the other on the original Afghanistan inquiry, which also looked at alleged war crimes by U.S. troops but has shifted towards looking at the ISIS-K militia.
Judges said they had taken the decision to close part of the case because prosecutors had not shown they would be able to effectively investigate allegations in Afghanistan apart from the Taliban probe. The splitting of the cases means the arrest warrants issued against four Afghan Taliban leaders remain in effect.
It is unclear if formally closing part of the Afghanistan case will be enough to allay American fears over the court exerting jurisdiction over U.S. nationals, as it does not change the court’s founding statute. The statute says the court can prosecute anyone accused of atrocity crimes committed on the territory of ICC member states.

articles.title: Italy boosts GCAP fighter spending as Army vehicles take a hit in budget
articles.snippet: Italy has hiked its spending on the GCAP fighter this year while reducing funding for new army tanks and fighting vehicles, newly released spending documents have revealed.
articles.full_text:
ROME — Italy has hiked its spending on the GCAP fighter this year while reducing funding for new army tanks and fighting vehicles, newly released spending documents have revealed.
Rome has spent €875 million ($970 million) in 2026 on GCAP – the program for a sixth-generation fighter which teams Italy with the United Kingdom and Japan.
That is up on last year’s €625 million and far higher than the €275 million that planners writing in last year’s budget document predicted would be spent in 2026.
The new numbers are contained in the much delayed Italian defense budget for 2026, which was sent by the defense ministry to parliament this week for approval.
Defense News has seen the part of the document containing the breakdown on costs per program, but not the section listing total spending.
The GCAP nations in July handed a £4.6 billion ($6.1 billion) development contract to their national champions building the jet after the U.K. freed up delayed cash.
The 18-month contract went to Edgewing, the industrial consortium grouping the firms building the fighter. Germany is reportedly now mulling signing up after the collapse of its plan to build the FCAS jet with France.
The 2026 budget document, which contains spending forecasts, predicts Italy will spend €696 million on the GCAP program in 2027.
Meanwhile spending on heavy army vehicles in 2026 was lower than forecast, despite Italy working on a new main battle tank and fighting vehicle with Rheinmetall.
The program envisages the delivery of 1,050 Lynx vehicles and 272 Panther tanks as part of a €23 billion euro deal. But in July, Italian defense minister Guido Crosetto said Italy would cut 18% in costs from the program.
The new document puts spending on the two new programs, as well as upgrades to Italy’s ageing Ariete tanks, at €177 million in 2026, lower than last year’s €281 million and far lower than the €425 million that last year’s document predicted would be spent in 2026.
By way of compensation, this year’s budget predicts a major hike in spending on the three programs to €872 million in 2027.
Although Defense News has not seen the section of the budget giving total expenditures, a tally of the costs of the individual program outlays this year amounts to €12.8 billion, up by €307 million from the €12.5 billion given by totaling all the programs in the 2025 budget.
Italy’s F-35 program, which involves the eventual purchase of 115 aircraft, cost Italy €782 million in 2026, less than the the €961 million planners last year forecast it would receive.
This year’s budget document has been the focus of heated political debate as defense spending comes under the spotlight ahead of Italian national elections next year, which will see incumbent right wing prime minister Giorgia Meloni seeking reelection.
Meloni’s arguments in favor of defense spending have come under fire from both her allies and foes, including Matteo Salvini, the head of League party which forms part of Meloni’s coalition, and Robert Vannacci, a former army general running a new party to the right of Meloni.
Among opposition parties, the Five Star party has also criticized defense spending, claiming they are diverting scarce funds from health spending.
Students who have recently taken to the streets in Italy as part of a Europe-wide wave of street protests have listed a cut to arms spending as one of their main aims.
The opposition to arms spending has coincided with growing opposition to supplying arms to Ukraine, a policy Meloni has fought for since her election in 2022.

articles.title: US Army names officer held on ‘allegations of espionage’
articles.snippet: Lt. Col. Brandon Carroll Tyner has been identified as the U.S. soldier arrested earlier this week in the UK for reportedly assisting Russian intelligence.
articles.full_text:
An Army official identified Lt. Col. Brandon Carroll Tyner as the U.S. soldier arrested earlier this week in the United Kingdom for reportedly assisting Russian intelligence in what FBI Director Kash Patel described as “allegations of espionage.”
Tyner, 41, began serving in the Army as a human resources officer — military occupational specialty 42H — in January 2008, the official told Military Times. Tyner’s deployments included tours in Afghanistan, Qatar and Iraq.
At the time of his arrest, he was assigned to Imjin Barracks, a British Army base near Gloucestershire, England, which hosts NATO’s Allied Rapid Reaction Corps. His arrest came shortly after the U.S. removed aircraft from British military bases over an unrelated reported threat from Iran.
Tyner was arrested under Sections 1 and 3 of Britain’s 2023 National Security Act and the Army said officials were investigating two locations in Gloucestershire. Counter Terrorism Policing London is leading the investigation and the accused officer remains in custody at a London police station.
“This important arrest involves allegations of espionage, which is of the utmost concern to the United States and our allies,” Patel said in a statement, adding that the FBI had made 167 counterintelligence and espionage arrests over the last 21 months.
Brig. Gen. Sean Stinchon, the commanding general of U.S. Army Counterintelligence Command, thanked the FBI authorities in the UK and encouraged anyone who notices something suspicious to consult officials.
“The alleged conduct of a senior soldier, entrusted with sensitive information, is a sobering reminder that insider threats are real and persistent. I encourage anyone who thinks they’ve witnessed something suspicious to report it to their local counterintelligence office,” he said in a statement.
The arrest comes amid U.S. European Command’s “See Something, Do Something” campaign, which calls on troops, family members and civilian employees to be vigilant about their digital presence and report unusual behavior to authorities. Though the campaign did not identify a specific threat, experts have warned that Russia is ramping up its hybrid warfare.
The Armed Conflict Location & Event Data Project, known as ACLED, said in an October report that Russia had increased its hybrid threats across Europe — such as targeting aviation in Germany, attempting to sabotage critical infrastructure in Poland and ramping up drone incursions in Romania and Moldova — in an attempt to weaken the region’s support for Ukraine. The report expects those threats to grow, noting that Moscow would likely use cyberattacks and ramp up attacks against defense and transportation infrastructure.

articles.title: Turkey and Egypt weigh joint naval shipbuilding projects
articles.snippet: Turkey and Egypt are taking steps to strengthen their cooperation in the maritime domain, with joint shipbuilding opportunities on the table.
articles.full_text:
ISTANBUL — Turkey and Egypt are taking steps to strengthen their cooperation in the maritime domain, with joint shipbuilding opportunities on the table.
Adm. Ercüment Tatlıoğlu, the commander of Turkey’s navy, made an announcement to that effect during the Sea of Friendship 2026 naval exercise in Alexandria, Egypt.
The exercise was conducted under the command of Egypt’s Northern Fleet from Nov. 4 to Nov. 9. The previous iteration took place in 2025, following a 13-year hiatus.
The largest warship in the Turkish Navy’s inventory, the amphibious assault ship TCG Anadolu, was among the Turkish units participating in the exercise. The drill covered surface warfare, anti-submarine warfare, air defense operations and underwater assault training.
Tatlıoğlu held talks with his Egyptian counterpart, Vice Adm. Mahmoud Adel Fawzy, on the sidelines of the event at Alexandria Naval Base on Nov. 7.
Tatlıoğlu described the Sea of Friendship exercise as a substantial demonstration of growing cooperation between Turkey and Egypt in the Eastern Mediterranean. He said the two navies were taking concrete steps to expand cooperation in unmanned aerial and naval systems, highlighting the participation of the Bayraktar TB3 unmanned aerial vehicle and the MKE Pirana one-way unmanned surface vehicle.
“We aim to take our defense industry cooperation in the maritime domain to a more advanced level by undertaking joint shipbuilding activities with Egypt, similar to the cooperation we have established with Pakistan under the MILGEM Project,” Tatlıoğlu said.
The MILGEM Project was initiated by the Turkish Navy to design and build indigenously developed naval platforms. The project has resulted in the development of Ada-class corvettes and Istanbul-class frigates, which are in service with the Turkish Navy, as well as Ada-class variants for the Pakistani, Ukrainian and Malaysian navies and a Hisar-class offshore patrol vessel for the Romanian Navy.
Meanwhile, Fawzy described this month’s exercise as well planned and executed despite sea conditions that were not particularly favorable.
“This activity demonstrates that we are on the right track,” he said. “We can train together, plan together and conduct ship-boarding activities together. We can work together. In the near future, the Egyptian and Turkish navies may be able to operate side by side, shoulder to shoulder, on joint missions.”
The naval exercise took place just 15 days after the House of Representatives in eastern Libya, based in Benghazi, unanimously ratified a Turkey–Libya maritime jurisdiction agreement on Oct 20.
The original 2019 Turkey-Libya maritime delimitation agreement is strategically important as it establishes a boundary between the two countries’ claimed continental shelves and exclusive economic zones (EEZs) in the Eastern Mediterranean.
For Turkey, this agreement is to protect its maritime jurisdiction claims and prevent Greek islands from effectively limiting Turkey’s access to maritime areas. For Libya, it provides a basis for asserting its own maritime rights.
Greece opposes the agreement, arguing that it disregards the maritime entitlements of Greek islands and undermines its claims in the Eastern Mediterranean.
In 2019, the agreement was signed only by Libya’s Government of National Accord in Tripoli. Now it has been ratified by the House of Representatives in Benghazi, thus bringing the two major parties in Libya to accept the agreement.
Even so, Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty described the pact as “completely null and void” during an Oct. 23 visit to Istanbul, where he met his Turkish counterpart, Hakan Fidan.
Serhat Güvenç, a professor of international relations at Kadir Has University in Istanbul, stated that Egypt was still unwilling to sign an agreement on exclusive economic zones (EEZs) with Turkey but was, at the same time, cooperating with Turkey in a major naval exercise in which TCG Anadolu was also participating.
“Egypt’s position regarding the Memorandum of Understanding signed with Libya and its willingness to develop military and maritime relations with Türkiye are not mutually exclusive,” he said. “In fact, in this picture, Egypt may perhaps be in a better position than the other actors in terms of respect for international law and acting with due care in this regard, because Turkey and Greece are pursuing maximalist positions.”

articles.title: Democrats push to remove US-Israel tech measure from defense bill
articles.snippet: The measures call for enhanced cooperation between the U.S. and Israel on weapons technology development.
articles.full_text:
Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., is leading a push to remove provisions from the Senate and House versions of this year’s National Defense Authorization Act that would promote closer ties between the U.S. industrial base and Israel’s.
A letter sent Tuesday to House and Senate leadership signed by Van Hollen and 11 other Senate colleagues, including Sens. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and Tammy Duckworth, D-Ill., specifically addresses Section 1217 of the Senate version and Section 219 of the House version of the bill.
Those sections, called the United States-Israel Defense Cooperation Initiative in the House and the United States-Israel Framework for Upgraded Technologies, Unified Research, and Enhanced Security (FUTURES) Act in the Senate, each call for enhanced cooperation between the two countries on weapons technology development, including in artificial intelligence, quantum technology and chemical and biological weapons.
“The Senator is working with his colleagues to remove these provisions and will determine next steps should they remain in,” Van Hollen’s office said in an email to Military Times. “The Senator will continue to push to remove these provisions and push to protect the United States’ ability to act independently and in line with U.S. national security interests.”
The letter also addresses a provision of the fiscal 2027 Intelligence Authorization Act that proposes enhancing intelligence-sharing between the two countries, which, according to the text of the bill, is intended to help Israel “maintain its qualitative military edge” and “deter and counter destabilizing activities by the Government of Iran and Iran-aligned state and nonstate actors that threaten Israel, United States forces, and regional partners.”
The U.S. government’s support for Israel has come under intense scrutiny over the past three years. Israel’s war in Gaza has killed at least 74,000 Palestinians, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry, and U.S. and Israeli attacks against Iran on Feb. 28 led to a war that’s increasingly unpopular in the United States, a new Reuters/Ipsos poll found.
President Donald Trump promised to end outright military aid to Israel, which has previously come via a Memorandum of Understanding. The current MOU is set to expire in 2028 and provides billions in financing for Israel to procure U.S.-made weapons over the 10-year agreement.
Critics, including Van Hollen, have noted that the annual defense bills, as they stand, merely shift military provision from an aid model to a commercial partnership, this time overseen by the Pentagon rather than the State Department.
The new model, as proposed in the draft legislation, “would constrain the administration’s ability to independently determine how best to protect U.S. national security and would lock in long-term commitments despite our serious concerns with the Israeli government’s actions in Gaza, the West Bank, and other parts of the region,” the letter states.
The U.S. and Israel already cooperate on some defense technology; Israeli contractor Rafael Systems and Raytheon developed the David’s Sling missile interceptor system. But critics say that the proposed setup would decrease oversight of the weapons transfer system; could compromise sensitive U.S. weapons technology; and wouldn’t provide much benefit for the United States.
The NDAA is one of Congress’s “must-pass” bills, but the price tag alone — more than $1 trillion — has drawn significant pushback from Democrats. The House’s version narrowly passed in July, and Senate Democrats blocked that chamber’s version the same month, objecting to provisions for the Iran war.
In the House, Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., tried unsuccessfully to pass an amendment striking the United States-Israel Defense Cooperation Initiative when the bill was being debated in committee. Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., was also a vocal opponent.

articles.title: House passes bill to expand benefits for combat-injured veterans
articles.snippet: The House approved legislation Thursday that would allow combat-injured military retirees with less than 20 years of service to collect their full military retirement pay and Department of Veterans Affairs disability compensation.
articles.full_text:
The House approved legislation Thursday that would allow combat-injured military retirees with less than 20 years of service to collect their full military retirement pay and Department of Veterans Affairs disability compensation without the dollar-for-dollar offset that currently reduces their retirement benefits.
The passage of the Major Richard Star Act, H.R. 2102, sends the measure to the Senate, where lawmakers must still approve it before it can reach the president’s desk.
The vote followed a months-long effort led by Rep. Mark Takano, D-Calif., ranking Democrat on the House Veterans’ Affairs Committee, to force consideration of the standalone legislation.
On May 21, Takano and Rep. Raul Ruiz, D-Calif., began an effort to force a House vote on a resolution that would set the rules for bringing the Major Richard Star Act to the floor. The petition reached the required 218 signatures on Sept. 15, with Rep. Nancy Mace, R-S.C., providing the decisive endorsement.
On Thursday, lawmakers adopted H. Res. 1247 by a 271-135 vote, clearing the way for final consideration of the Star Act.
Rep. Joe Courtney, D-Conn., who signed the discharge petition, urged the Senate to act following Thursday’s passage.
“By finally passing the Major Richard Star Act, a bipartisan coalition just took a major step to follow through on that mission,” Courtney said in a Nov. 12 statement. He urged senators to send it to the president.
The bill’s Republican sponsor, Rep. Gus Bilirakis, R-Fla., introduced the legislation in 2020. Ruiz and Takano have been leading Democratic advocates for its passage.
Veterans of Foreign Wars National Commander-in-Chief Corey Geisler emphasized that securing a vote was not enough without passage of the full legislation.
“Getting a vote is not the finish line,” Geisler said. “Passing the right bill is.”
Following Thursday’s passage, Wounded Warrior Project applauded the House vote and called on the Senate to act.
“We thank House Veterans’ Affairs Committee Ranking Member Mark Takano and Congressman Raul Ruiz for their efforts to advance the discharge petition, Congressman Gus Bilirakis for his longstanding commitment to the bipartisan Major Richard Star Act, and the members of the House of Representatives for taking an important step toward providing long-overdue relief for combat-injured veterans,” said Jose Ramos, the organization’s senior vice president of government and community relations.
The Senate companion, S. 1032, remains before the Senate Armed Services Committee. The Senate has no equivalent to the House discharge-petition process, and previous attempts to advance the measure by unanimous consent were blocked by objections. The Senate must still approve the legislation before it can be passed.

articles.title: Delivering first Columbia-class sub in 2028 is ‘absolutely achievable’, sub czar says
articles.snippet: Vice Adm. Rob Gaucher, the direct reporting portfolio manager for Submarines, said that delivering the first Columbia-class submarine in 2028 is still a ‘heavy lift.’
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON — Delivering the first Columbia-class submarine by the Navy’s 2028 goal is doable — although not an “easy” task, the Pentagon’s first-ever submarine czar said today, seemingly offering a more optimistic outlook on his previously shared view of the goal.
Vice Adm. Rob Gaucher, the Direct Reporting Portfolio Manager (DPRM) for Submarines, said in April that hitting the 2028 target would amount to a “wicked heavy lift.” Today, however, he said the goal is “absolutely achievable” amid an increase in operations in recent months.
“To be clear, delivering District of Columbia in 2028 is still not easy, so it does remain a heavy lift, and we have plenty of work to do,” Gaucher said during the Submarine League Annual Symposium today. “But it is absolutely achievable. My confidence grows each week as we review deck plate performance, align on goals, improve our production planning, and address day-to-day production bottlenecks.”
This is a more optimistic view of the goal from April when Gaucher said they still needed to work through “hiccups” since the submarine had never been operated before. He further said at the time that a 2028 delivery time would not be met if it meant long-term consequences for the program.
Although the first Columbia-class submarine, the District of Columbia, was first slated for delivery in 2027, Navy leaders said in 2025 that the delivery date could shift to 2029 amid supplier issues. Even so, Navy leaders have consistently said this year that they are aiming for a 2028 delivery date for the submarine.
That estimate comes after the Navy and its shipbuilding partners who are building the District of Columbia, General Dynamics Electric Boat and HII’s Newport News Shipbuilding, established an acceleration plan in 2025 to deliver all modules for the Columbia-class submarine to the final assembly yard at General Dynamic Electric Boat in Groton, Conn., by the end of 2025.
Rear Adm. Todd Weeks, then the program executive officer for strategic submarines, said at the WEST 2026 conference in February that the acceleration plan had resulted in a construction “ramp-up” for the Columbia-class, and that full-rate construction of the vessel was slated for the early 2030s.
Weeks, who is now the portfolio acquisition executive for industrial operations, said at the time that the District of Columbia was approximately 65 percent complete, and that the second Columbia-class submarine, the future Wisconsin, was roughly 35 percent complete.
The Navy initially stated in 2024 that several shipbuilding programs were suffering from delays due to shipyard workforce and supply chain challenges, and as a result, reported that the District of Columbia was expected to face a 12 to 16-month delivery delay.
